opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think our position is a bit unusual, and in some ways quite fortunate.

vLLM didn't start as a company. It started as a research project at Berkeley, and it grew because a lot of people found it useful and decided to contribute. So by the time we started thinking seriously about a company, there was already a very large community: model labs, hardware vendors, cloud providers, and many individual developers all running vLLM in production. That's something you can't really buy or manufacture. It took years of people trusting the project with real workloads.

So when I think about our position, the first thing is that we sit at a kind of crossroads. On one side you have the model developers, who release new architectures almost every month, with new attention variants, mixture-of-experts, multimodal inputs, very long context. On the other side you have the hardware: NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPUs, and many new accelerators, including domestic chips. Inference is where these two sides meet, and vLLM has become a common layer between them. Model teams often work with us to get day-zero support, and hardware vendors want their chips to run vLLM well because that's what their customers already use. That middle position is our main asset.

At the same time, I'm cautious about how we use that position. The biggest risk for a company built around an open-source project is that it starts to treat the community as something to extract from. If people feel the project is being steered only for one company's commercial interest, the trust disappears, and with it the thing that made the project valuable. So our principle is that the open-source project has to stay genuinely open and neutral, and the company has to earn its place by contributing more than anyone else, not by controlling it.

Commercially, I think the opportunity is real. Inference is becoming the dominant cost of AI. Training is a big, one-time investment, but inference grows with every user and every agent call, and now with reasoning models and agents the number of tokens is exploding. Many enterprises want to run models themselves, for cost, privacy, or customization reasons, but making inference fast, cheap, and reliable at scale is hard. There's a lot of engineering between "the model runs" and "the model runs efficiently on a large cluster with good latency and utilization." That gap is where a company can provide value: deep optimization, support, deployment at scale, and helping people adopt new hardware.

I'll also be honest that the competition is strong. There are other excellent open-source inference engines, the big cloud providers have their own stacks, and the hardware companies are investing heavily in software too. So we can't rely on being first. We have to keep moving fast, keep the architecture clean enough that the community can keep extending it, and stay close to the frontier models.

So in summary, I'd say our position is strong because of the community and the neutral role we play in the ecosystem, but that strength is something we have to keep earning. If we do it right, I think the company and the open-source project can reinforce each other rather than compete.

r001.rationale: The response describes the team’s position as unusual and fortunate, grounded in vLLM’s years of community trust and production use—an advantage it says cannot be bought or manufactured. This communicates that other prospective founders would not necessarily have had the same positioning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that we didn't start from "let's build a company around vLLM." We started from the project itself.

vLLM began as an academic project at Berkeley, and most of us who became core maintainers came in as contributors first. I was doing my PhD at Tsinghua, working on things like PyTorch compilation and distributed inference, and I started contributing because the problems were genuinely interesting and the project was moving fast. Over time, a group of us ended up carrying a lot of the day-to-day responsibility: reviews, releases, hardware support, the compiler integration, the performance work. At some point, the community was large enough that it needed people whose full-time job was to keep it healthy.

So I think of our position less as "a startup that owns vLLM" and more as "a team that is accountable to vLLM." That distinction matters to us. The project is open source, it's governed openly, and a lot of the contributions come from companies that are, frankly, much bigger than we are. If we behaved as if the project belonged to us, we would lose exactly the thing that makes it valuable.

Where a company fits is in the gap between the open-source project and what production users actually need. The open-source version is excellent, but running inference at scale is still painful: multi-node deployments, heterogeneous hardware, cost control, observability, keeping up with every new model architecture that comes out each week. That is a lot of operational burden, and most teams don't want to build it themselves. We can take on that burden because we understand the internals better than anyone, and we can push improvements back upstream rather than forking.

There is also a timing argument. Inference is becoming the dominant cost in AI, and the hardware landscape is fragmenting: NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPUs, domestic Chinese chips, custom ASICs. A neutral, open inference layer that works across all of them is valuable to everyone, including the hardware vendors. We're in a good position to be that neutral layer precisely because we're not tied to any single vendor or model lab.

The risk, of course, is the classic open-source tension: if you give away too much, there's no business; if you hold back too much, the community moves on. Our bet is that the project's momentum is the moat, and that keeping the core fully open is the only way to keep that momentum. We'll find out whether that bet is right, but it's the one I'm comfortable making.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the team understands vLLM’s internals “better than anyone,” which clearly conveys that other potential founders would not necessarily be as well positioned.

astra-6.text: I think we’re in a good position technically because we work closely on vLLM and understand the challenges of serving models efficiently. But that doesn’t automatically mean we’re in a good position to build a company. You still have to understand what customers need, what they’re willing to pay for, and how to deliver something reliable. So I see the technical foundation as a starting advantage. The real question is whether we can turn that into a product that solves a clear problem while continuing to support the open-source project.

r001.rationale: The response says the team has a technical advantage from working closely on vLLM, but does not compare its position with that of other potential founders.

The real question is what problem customers need us to solve and whether we can build a sustainable business around that. We’d also want to keep contributing to the open-source project, because that community is a big part of what makes vLLM valuable.
